llmRouter.title: LLM Router
llmRouter.tagline: Single entry, intelligent dispatch to multiple inference pools
llmRouter.introStory: Enterprises front multiple inference stacks with one BIG-IP VS and one OpenAI-compatible URL. iRuleLX parses each request, selects a pool from the routing table, upgrades by context size when needed, and will retry or fall back when backends fail.
llmRouter.overviewNote: All four sub-features are live: model routing, context-size routing, agent routing, and Retry/Fallback resilience.
bullets: Model Based Routing: map model names to inference Pools
Context Size Routing: steer by serialized messages size across small/large Pools
Agent/Subagent Routing: specialized agents, one API—F5 routes by agent identity to the right pool
Retry & Fallback: retry or switch to backup Pools on failure

observability.tagline: LLM observability aligned with the live Prometheus pipeline
observability.introStory: This demo now mirrors the real collection and computation path: BIG-IP iRuleLX emits structured events, the Adapter receives `/events`, performs request_id dedup, pricing, and metric aggregation, exposes `/metrics` for Prometheus scrape, and Grafana renders live dashboards for requests, tokens, latency, retry/fallback, and cost.

Core metrics: RPS, error ratio, Retry/Fallback ratio, TTFT/Latency quantiles, Prompt/Completion tokens, and cost
Dashboard filters match live variables: model, pool, member, client_ip, and price_version

retryFallback.title: Retry & Fallback
retryFallback.tagline: When the primary pool fails, retry or steer to a backup without client changes
retryFallback.introStory: Inference clusters can be briefly unavailable during upgrades, maintenance, upstream throttling, or sudden failures. When apps point directly at a single backend, one outage becomes a user-visible error or long wait. Retry and Fallback adds a second safety net at the gateway: when the primary pool struggles, traffic is retried or steered to a backup pool—apps keep the same API URL and gain higher continuity without code changes.
bullets: Brief primary-pool glitches often mean a slightly longer wait—not an immediate failure—reducing perceived outages from infrastructure noise
When the primary pool stays down, traffic can fall back to a preconfigured backup pool so critical work continues within the failure window
Retry and fallback policies live in one gateway configuration—apps need not each implement their own retry logic or drift on policy
Stacks with model routing, context upgrade, and agent steering for a full “routing + resilience” gateway story
techFeatures: With Retry enabled, iRuleLX Orchestrator runs an attempt queue: limited retries on the primary pool (5xx/429), then fallback pool
Each attempt goes through Layered VS sideband; TCP LB_FAILED triggers in-pool reselect; exhausted members trigger cross-pool fallback via iRule
Demo A: model=testmodel triggers status-code retry—watch request counter delta and final fallback to pool_llm_default
Demo B: dead member 7999 in pool_deepseek-chat reselects to 8005; all members offline triggers cross-pool fallback
explain: Status-code scenario: request model=testmodel, hit pool_testmode, then retry and fallback to pool_llm_default
If fallback pool is also unavailable, BIG-IP may return x-llm-retry-terminal=1 with upstream_error
TCP scenario: pool_deepseek-chat has dead member 7999 and healthy member 8005, system should reselect to 8005
After forcing 8005 offline, requests should fallback to default pool
retryFallback.opsNoteBody: The interactive demo uses F5 iControl REST to prepare member states before each run, so prior test residue does not break the scenario.

obsTokens.title: Token usage
obsTokens.tagline: See how much each team spends on AI—fuel FinOps and budget control
obsTokens.introStory: After rolling out Copilot and AI assistants at scale, leadership asks: how many tokens did each team use, what did it cost, and is the trend under control? Without unified observability, finance reconciles vendor consoles one by one—hard to charge back or warn before overrun. This scene shows how the F5 gateway feeds every LLM call’s token usage and cost into one dashboard for FinOps and ops to drill down by model, department, and application.
bullets: Pull scattered backend usage into one dashboard for department and application chargeback and budget management
Track per-model token trends in real time and catch spikes or abuse before the month-end bill surprise
Separate prompt vs completion tokens to see whether cost comes from long inputs or verbose outputs—and tune accordingly
Cost by price_version keeps historical spend comparable when model pricing or contracts change
techFeatures: iRuleLX emits structured llm_request_completed events with model/pool/member/usage fields on each finished request
Observability Adapter ingests /events, deduplicates, prices via pricing_rules.json, and writes Prometheus counters
Core metrics: llm_prompt_tokens_total, llm_completion_tokens_total, llm_cost_total with model/pool/member/client_ip labels
Grafana drills down with shared variables; this page can start simulated traffic to refresh metrics

obsMetrics.title: Model metrics
obsMetrics.tagline: When users say “AI feels slow”—find which model and which server
obsMetrics.introStory: When users report slowness or frequent errors, ops must quickly tell which model, pool, or server is at fault. Backend logs alone rarely tie routing decisions to performance. This scene shows how F5 exports request volume, error rates, time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, and retry/fallback behavior into one metric stream so Grafana can surface bottlenecks and stability risks at a glance.
bullets: Drill from “it feels slow” to a specific model, pool, or member—shorter mean time to diagnose
Watch success, retry, and fallback rates together to separate backend performance from routing/resilience triggers
TTFT vs end-to-end latency shows whether delay is queue/generation or network/gateway overhead
Filter by client_ip, model, pool, and more for capacity planning, SLA review, and peak-hour operations
techFeatures: Adapter exports llm_requests_total (with status label) plus retry/fallback counters from iRuleLX structured events
Latency via histograms: llm_ttft_ms_bucket (first token) and llm_latency_ms_bucket (end-to-end)
Grafana computes p95 and similar percentiles with model/pool/member/client_ip filters
Same Adapter source as the Tokens sub-scene—traffic, performance, and cost on one dashboard

trafficMgmt.title: Optimization and Control
trafficMgmt.tagline: Optimize inference resource use and control agent tool access at the unified gateway
trafficMgmt.introStory: After LLM Router picks a pool, two optimization and control needs remain: avoid hot GPUs inside a model pool, and safely connect agents to many MCP tool servers in Agentic AI workloads. Optimization and Control covers both—TBLB for intelligent in-pool inference scheduling, and MCP Tools Call Insight / Control for observability and policy-governed tool access (planned).
trafficMgmt.overviewNote: TBLB, model allow/block, and max_tokens ceiling demos are live; MCP Tools Call Insight / Control are planned placeholders.
bullets: Intelligent inference scheduling (TBLB): after Router picks a pool, steer to the best GPU member from live metrics
Model allow/block list: model admission at the unified gateway—prevent agents from calling costly or unapproved models
max_tokens ceiling: iRule Layer 0 caps per-request max_tokens to stop agents from requesting excessive generation length
MCP Tools Call Control (planned): unified MCP tool access, auth, rate limits, and routing policy at the gateway

tblb.title: LLM Router + Intelligent Inference Scheduling (TBLB)
tblb.tagline: Router selects the right model pool; TBLB selects the best GPU member in that pool
tblb.introStory: After routing by model, many GPUs often serve the same pool. Classic round-robin or least-connections cannot see long queues or full KV caches—users hit the same model entry yet may land on the busiest card, so responses feel uneven. After Router picks the pool, TBLB reads live queue and cache metrics on each GPU and steers each request to the lightest member expected to respond fastest—avoiding hot GPUs without users changing URLs, improving peak stability and consistency.
bullets: With multiple GPUs behind one model entry, steer away from the longest queues and fullest caches—fewer “sometimes fast, sometimes forever” moments
Apps keep one model name and gateway URL; scaling GPUs stays transparent to upstream teams
At peak, send new work to freer inference nodes—less hot-GPU overload and better overall utilization
Layers with Router pool choice and Retry/Fallback: Router picks capability class; TBLB picks which server inside the pool
techFeatures: LLM Router steers by model to pools such as pool_gpt-4o, pool_gemini-1.5-pro, and pool_deepseek-chat
gpt-4o and gemini-1.5-pro pools run TBLB Scheduler on vLLM/SGLang queue, cache, and in-flight metrics
Scheduler S1/S2 algorithms weight metrics into per-member percent and pick the best GPU per request
pool_deepseek-chat uses standard pool LB (no TBLB); connection failure triggers in-pool reselect, coordinated with Router retry/fallback

modelAllowlist.title: Model allow/block one-click control
modelAllowlist.tagline: Govern which models may be used at the unified gateway—stop agents from calling costly or unapproved models
modelAllowlist.introStory: After rolling out Copilot, coding agents, and other AI apps, enterprises often operate multiple purchased or self-hosted models with different permissions and cost budgets by team and use case. If every app or agent can freely set the model name on each request, teams may bypass approval and invoke flagship models—driving runaway spend, compliance violations, and vendor-policy conflicts. Platform teams need model admission at the unified LLM gateway: only approved models enter the inference path; unauthorized or high-risk models are rejected, and policy changes should apply centrally without redeploying every application. Model allow/block control validates the model field on every request at the gateway—like checking a badge before entry: no badge, no access.
bullets: Stop agents and apps from arbitrarily choosing expensive, unpurchased, or unapproved models—control inference cost and vendor compliance at the source
Maintain model admission policy centrally on the gateway—add, retire, or temporarily block a model once and it applies everywhere, without changing each business app
Reject unauthorized requests before they reach inference—avoid wasted GPU capacity and accidental use of high-privilege models on sensitive workloads
techFeatures: iRule Layer 0 (ir_openai_api.tcl): parse model from JSON body, lookup dg_openai_model_list
Data Group values are allow or block; misses use DEFAULT_MODEL_ACTION (block in this demo)
BLOCK mode returns HTTP 403 with OpenAI-compatible error JSON
Same System Prompt VS (172.16.30.124:8000); allow list includes demo-model, gpt-5.2-codex, gpt-5.3-codex
explain: Left panel shows datagroup rules and policy preview; send a request to see allow or block on the right
demo-model, gpt-5.2-codex, and gpt-5.3-codex are allow in dg_openai_model_list—expect HTTP 200
Any model not explicitly allowed (e.g. gpt-4o) hits default block—expect HTTP 403
If results differ, verify JSON Profile + iRule on the VS and datagroup matches this demo config
modelAllowlist.policyNoteBody: dg_openai_model_list: demo-model / gpt-5.2-codex / gpt-5.3-codex → allow; DEFAULT_MODEL_ACTION = block. Only these models may proceed; others are stopped at iRule Layer 0.
modelAllowlist.opsTip: Ops tip: tmsh modify ltm data-group internal dg_openai_model_list records add { demo-model { data allow } gpt-5.2-codex { data allow } gpt-5.3-codex { data allow } }; DEFAULT_MODEL_ACTION is set in iRule variables.

maxTokensLimit.title: max_tokens ceiling control
maxTokensLimit.tagline: Cap per-request generation length at the gateway—stop agents from setting excessive max_tokens
maxTokensLimit.introStory: Agents and Copilots can set max_tokens on each request to cap how many tokens the model may generate. Without governance, a single call with thousands or tens of thousands of max_tokens can burn GPU capacity and budget and slow shared inference clusters. Enterprises need a unified “per-request generation budget” at the LLM gateway—requests above MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT are rejected before they reach inference (alternatively, max_tokens may be automatically clamped to the limit and allowed through), with policy applied centrally.
bullets: Stop agents from setting excessive max_tokens on a single request—control inference cost and GPU usage at the source
Set the ceiling once at the gateway—business apps do not need their own validation logic
Over-limit requests are rejected at iRule Layer 0 (or max_tokens may be auto-clamped to the limit and forwarded)—avoid wasted compute and protect backend stability
techFeatures: iRule Layer 0 (ir_openai_api.tcl): parse max_tokens from JSON body and compare to MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT
Demo MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT = 4096; default BLOCK mode returns HTTP 403 when exceeded (optional: rewrite max_tokens to the limit and forward)
Same iRule Layer 0 as model admission; demo uses demo-model (allow in dg_openai_model_list)
Shares System Prompt VS (172.16.30.124:8000) and JSON Profile
explain: Click “Run compare demo”: sends max_tokens=2048 (compliant) and 8192 (overflow) in parallel—side-by-side allow vs 403 (this demo uses BLOCK; optional auto-clamp mode available)
2048 ≤ 4096 should return HTTP 200; 8192 > 4096 should return HTTP 403 in BLOCK mode (or auto-clamp max_tokens and allow)
Use custom max_tokens or “at limit / over by 1” quick buttons for boundary tests
If the overflow card is not 403, verify F5 iRule MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT=4096 and demo-model model admission
maxTokensLimit.policyNoteBody: MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT = 4096; model = demo-model (allow). max_tokens ≤ 4096 allowed; > 4096 returns 403 at iRule Layer 0 (or max_tokens may be auto-clamped to 4096 and forwarded). This demo uses BLOCK reject mode.
maxTokensLimit.opsTip: Ops tip: MAX_TOKENS_LIMIT is set in iRule variables; over-limit may BLOCK with 403 or optionally auto-clamp max_tokens to the limit and forward.

mcpToolsInsight.title: MCP Tools Call Insight
mcpToolsInsight.tagline: Visibility into MCP tool-call volume, distribution, and health
mcpToolsInsight.introStory: After Agentic AI rollouts, platform teams need answers: which agents call which MCP tools, whether volume is abnormal, where failures cluster, and whether peaks create hotspots. MCP Tools Call Insight collects structured tool-call events at the F5 gateway, aggregates them through the Adapter, and surfaces dashboards in Prometheus / Grafana by tool, agent, and tenant.
bullets: Capture latency, status, tool name, and agent identity for every MCP tool call in one place
Reuse the Observability Adapter + Prometheus + Grafana stack for side-by-side model and tool analysis
Trend call volume, success rate, and P95 latency by tool type, business line, and environment
Give security and compliance teams a traceable view of who called which tool and when
techFeatures: F5 gateway emits structured audit events from MCP JSON-RPC sessions (tool, agent, status, latency)
Adapter ingests tool-call events and exports Prometheus metrics (volume, error rate, latency quantiles)
Grafana dashboards drill down by tool / agent / tenant and correlate with LLM inference metrics
Planned: same collection path as llm_request_completed events to reduce ops overhead

mcpToolsControl.title: MCP Tools Call Control
mcpToolsControl.tagline: Unified MCP tool access and call policy at the gateway
mcpToolsControl.introStory: Agentic AI apps often call databases, knowledge bases, ticketing, code repos, and more via MCP. If every agent wires its own tool URLs and credentials, integration fragments and policy enforcement becomes hard. MCP Tools Call Control proxies MCP traffic at the F5 entry—routing, auth, rate limits, and fail-close—so agents see one gateway while the enterprise governs which tools are exposed and how they are called.
bullets: Agents and Copilots use one MCP gateway URL for approved tool servers—less integration and credential sprawl
Central auth, quotas, and rate limits at the gateway for compliant tool use
Route tool traffic by business line, environment, or agent identity for multi-tenant and staged rollouts
Fail-close and health-check policies keep unhealthy MCP servers from breaking agent workflows
techFeatures: F5 Virtual Server as MCP (HTTP/SSE) entry, proxying JSON-RPC sessions between agents and MCP server pools
Data Group or policy table maps tool name / server id → backend MCP server pool
Gateway enforces token auth, rate limits, and tool allowlists
Planned: Streamable HTTP / SSE long-lived sessions with member-level load balancing

security.title: LLM Security
security.tagline: Harden system prompts and integrate guardrails before traffic hits inference
security.introStory: Enterprise Copilot rollouts need protection against prompt injection and policy bypass. The gateway can inject or validate system prompts and call guardrail APIs before requests reach backends.
security.overviewNote: System prompt hardening and LLM Guardrail integration both have interactive demos.
bullets: System prompt hardening: enforce corporate system instructions
LLM Guardrail integration: content safety scan with gateway-side reject
Audit logs for policy hits and blocks

systemPrompt.title: System prompt hardening
systemPrompt.tagline: Ensure every request carries compliant system instructions users cannot override
systemPrompt.introStory: Enterprise Copilot apps must answer within approved policy and compliance frames. When system prompts live on the client, they can be tampered with, omitted, or overridden by user messages—models drift off corporate policy. System prompt hardening injects or validates enterprise system instructions at the gateway so every inference call runs under the same policy.
bullets: Every inference request carries approved enterprise system instructions—no client omission or tampering compliance gap
Users cannot bypass corporate safety and brand voice via crafted messages—lower prompt-injection and policy drift risk
Policy updates ship centrally at the gateway—business apps need not redeploy route-by-route for global effect
Policy hits and blocks feed the audit trail for regulated industries such as finance and healthcare
techFeatures: F5 v21 JSON Profile fires JSON_REQUEST; iRule merges and rewrites system-role messages
Three-layer XML wrapper: admin_prompts / untrusted user_prompts / final_guardrails (BIG-IP mandatory-rules block, iRule tag name)
Dynamic nonce tags (demo fixed to F5) block fake closing tags in user-supplied system prompts
Aligned with ir_openai_api.tcl: F5 BIG-IP mandatory enforcement rules can force YAML over Markdown in user_prompts
explain: Client sends untrusted system messages; F5 wraps them into one system blob on JSON_REQUEST
Mock LLM (demo-model @ 8011) parses the BIG-IP mandatory-rules block (final_guardrails_F5) and returns deterministic YAML
Format preset: user asks for Markdown, BIG-IP mandatory rules require YAML — response should be YAML
Injection preset: forged admin_prompts tags stay inside user_prompts_F5; mandatory rules still win
systemPrompt.formatNoteBody: Even when user system says "use Markdown", F5 BIG-IP mandatory enforcement rules (e.g. You MUST answer in yaml format) take priority; Mock LLM returns YAML.
systemPrompt.nonceNoteBody: Demo uses NONCE_RANDOM=0 and NONCE_LENGTH=1 (suffix F5). Attackers cannot predict tag names; fake </user_prompts> cannot close the real wrapper.
systemPrompt.opsTip: F5 logs: tail -f /var/log/ltm | grep JSON_REQUEST; set DEBUG_PROMPTS=1 to see before/after system text.

guardrails.title: LLM Guardrail integration
guardrails.tagline: Gate user input at your unified AI entry—violations stop at the edge, compliant traffic flows through
guardrails.introStory: When enterprises offer Copilot, intelligent support, or knowledge Q&A, a single policy-violating user prompt can trigger regulatory exposure, brand risk, and audit findings. If every application wires its own guardrail, policies diverge, integration cost multiplies, and security teams lose a single view of violations. Guardrails at the F5 unified gateway puts content safety in one place: every LLM call is checked against corporate policy before it reaches a model—rules that match are rejected immediately; compliant requests still get normal model answers, without per-app security rewrites.
bullets: Stop harmful or policy-violating user input at the unified entry before it reaches the model and spreads compliance risk
One corporate guardrail policy covers all Copilot and business apps—central updates take effect everywhere, cutting duplicate integration
Compliant conversations get normal responses; violations get a uniform rejection—user experience and security boundaries together
Block and allow outcomes leave an audit trail for security and compliance teams—trends, investigations, and alerting
techFeatures: Dual-VS design: Gateway VS (vs_guardrail_oob_gateway :8000) for clients; Egress VS (vs_guardrail_ssl_egress :8031) with Server SSL to Guardrail
Gateway iRule SIDEBAND to guardrail_egress_dest, POST {"input":"..."} to /backend/v1/scans, parse result.outcome
passed/cleared: force stream:false then forward Default Pool; flagged: return OpenAI block JSON (HTTP 200)
Settings in Data Group guardrail_oob_config: token, host, timeout, enable_request_scan—hot-reloadable
explain: Client POST /v1/chat/completions to Gateway VS; iRule extracts message text from JSON body
Sideband via Egress VS → pool_guardrail_aigr → HTTPS (SNI=us1.calypsoai.app) to Guardrail Scan API
On pass: rewrite body (stream→false) and forward Default Pool; on flagged: block without upstream forward
Demo default VS 172.16.30.120:8000, requests sent via local proxy with stream:true—compare block vs allow prompts
guardrails.blockNoteBody: When Guardrail returns flagged, Gateway responds HTTP 200 with OpenAI chat.completion JSON; choices[0].message.content cites F5 AI Guardrail policy violation—the request never hits the backend LLM pool.
guardrails.passNoteBody: On passed/cleared Gateway forwards to the Default Pool. If the client sent stream:true, the gateway forces non-stream before forward; the demo proxy consumes SSE and reports chunk count.
guardrails.proxyWhy: Browsers cannot reach lab VS addresses directly; the demo uses the local Python proxy, same as Model Based Routing and other sub-scenes.
guardrails.opsTip: F5 logs: tail -f /var/log/ltm | grep guardrail_oob; ensure guardrail_api_token and guardrail_egress_dest in the Data Group are correct.

modelRouting.title: Model Based Routing
modelRouting.tagline: One public front door—a smart operator that sends each AI model request to the right inference cluster
modelRouting.introStory: Enterprises often run GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and internal models in parallel—built by different teams, billed under different contracts, with different compliance boundaries. When every application points to its own backend URL, traffic is scattered: onboarding a new model means changing many apps, and operations cannot see who uses which model or where spend goes. Model Based Routing gives the business one AI gateway entry: apps call with familiar model names and the gateway steers each request to the right inference cluster—no per-app “model name → backend address” matrix to maintain.
bullets: Marketing, engineering, and support can each use the right model while all apps share one gateway URL—pick a model name and reach the matching inference service
New models and route changes are managed centrally at the gateway, not by redeploying every application—faster from procurement to production use
All model traffic passes one entry point, enabling usage reporting by department and application for chargeback, quotas, and compliance audit
Business teams keep calling with familiar model names; internal mapping and cutover stay transparent at the gateway, lowering integration and ops cost when many models coexist
techFeatures: Entry Virtual Server uses HTTP Profile plus iRuleLX (ILX Profile) to parse requests and make routing decisions at the gateway
Route map lives in a BIG-IP Data Group: key = request model, value = target Pool [, rewrite model [, extra field]]
__default__ key points to a fallback Pool when no rule matches, so unknown models still land predictably
Optional field2: rewrite the model field in the JSON body before forward so client aliases decouple from backend model names (demo highlights successful rewrites in violet)
explain: VS requires HTTP Profile and ILX Profile
Data Group value: field1[,field2[,field3]] — field1 is Pool, field2 is optional model rewrite
__default__ key is the fallback Pool when no match
When field2 applies, a 200 response model field may differ from the request model
modelRouting.modelRewriteNoteBody: When the Data Group value is "Pool,backendModel", iRuleLX updates the model field in the JSON body before forwarding. If the response is 200 and response model ≠ request model, the result card highlights the rewrite in violet.
modelRouting.proxyWhy: This demo proxies requests via Python to avoid browser CORS and unify timeouts/errors. The interactive panel calls /v1/chat/completions as an example only—it does not mean production clients must use that API shape.

contextRouting.title: Context Size Routing
contextRouting.tagline: The longer the working chat gets, the heavier the lift—quietly upgrade from quick answers to a large-context specialist
contextRouting.introStory: In IDEs, ticket systems, and knowledge Q&A, users start with short questions, then paste logs, documents, or spreadsheets—the conversation keeps growing. Always using a lightweight engine leads to fast replies until a long paste suddenly slows or truncates; always using a large-context engine wastes money on small talk. Context Size Routing steers by this request’s conversation weight at the gateway: routine chat on an economical pool, long-document work on a large-context pool—same model entry for users, smoother experience and smarter spend.
bullets: From “fix one line” to “paste the full stack trace”—same business API; the gateway upgrades to inference that can carry long context
Avoid the cliff where smooth chat suddenly times out or goes off-topic after one long paste
Light resources for short turns; expensive large-context capacity only when the payload truly needs it—FinOps-friendly by scenario
Stacks with model routing: recognize the business model first, then split by conversation length—like production’s “same brand, different load”
techFeatures: On top of Model Based Routing, Data Group field3 supports Size|threshold|large-context Pool|large-context model
Threshold compares serialized messages array byte length; demo uses 5k = 5×1024 = 5120 bytes
Under threshold: field1 pool + field2 model; over threshold: switch to field3 large pool/model
Multi-turn chats accumulate bytes per request; crossing the threshold switches pools without client parameter changes
explain: DG example: /Common/pool_deepseek-chat,deepseek-chat,Size|5k|pool_deepseek_v4|deepseek-v4-flash
5k in field3 means 5×1024=5120 bytes threshold on serialized messages array
Under threshold: field1 Pool + field2 model; over: largePool + largeModel
Multi-turn chats accumulate context; crossing 5k triggers Pool/model switch
contextRouting.calcNote: Use the slider to set target messages bytes. Multiturn sim sends before/after 5k requests with side-by-side highlighted results.

agentRouting.title: Agent/Subagent Based Routing
agentRouting.tagline: Many agents, different strengths—one API; F5 routes each role to the right pool
agentRouting.introStory: More enterprises orchestrate complex work with multiple AI agents. In an “AI coding assistant,” the supervisor coordinates the flow, the planner reads specs, the coder generates code, and testing and security scanning each need different strengths—each role should land on different inference resources. If every sub-agent keeps its own API URL and routing rules, the orchestration platform grows heavy and traffic/cost governance fragments. Agent Routing lets all agents share one API and gateway entry while declaring which agent is calling; F5 steers to the right pool—long context for planning, flagship models for coding, lightweight pools for security scan—balancing product flexibility with centralized operations.
bullets: Multi-agent orchestration maintains one API address; each role calls with an identity tag—lower integration and credential sprawl
Planning, coding, testing, and scanning need different model strengths—the gateway matches resources at forward time without per-agent backend URLs
Expose one enterprise alias such as EnterpriseAgentModel; internal per-pool model mapping stays transparent for upgrades and swaps
All agent traffic through one entry enables audit (“which role used which model”), quotas, and centralized route policy changes
techFeatures: Agent identity map lives in BIG-IP Data Group (llm_agent_pool_map), same mechanism as Model Based Routing
Identity from HTTP header (x-Agent-Identity), system message name, or model field set to the role name
Demo roles: superviser / planner / coder / tester / scanner, each routed to a different LTM pool
With header or system.name, field2 rewrite can expose EnterpriseAgentModel outward while forwarding each pool’s backend model name
explain: Business view: the orchestrator focuses on tasks and collaboration; model-to-pool mapping lives in BIG-IP Data Group (llm_agent_pool_map)
Technical view: F5 extracts identity from x-Agent-Identity, system message name, or model field (superviser / planner / coder / tester / scanner)
With header or system.name, clients may send EnterpriseAgentModel; F5 rewrites to the backend model the target pool expects
The interaction panel animates each sub-agent → F5 VS → pool; purple cards indicate an internal model rewrite
agentRouting.modelRewriteNote: One outward model name, correct model in each pool
agentRouting.modelRewriteNoteBody: Same as Model Based Routing: agents can call with a shared alias; F5 rewrites the JSON model before forwarding so each pool receives the name its backend accepts—no per-agent model string sprawl.
agentRouting.identityNote: How one API tells agents apart
agentRouting.identityNoteBody: Orchestrators need not swap URLs per role—only declare who is calling. The demo supports header (x-Agent-Identity), system message name, or model field as the role tag; F5 routes to the matching pool.

status.title: Scenario A: Target model returns 5xx/429 — auto Retry, then Fallback to default pool after repeated failures

status.retryTerminalHit: Terminal retry detected (x-llm-retry-terminal=1): both primary and fallback pools unavailable.

tcp.title: Scenario B: TCP failure triggers fallback
tcp.desc: First verify auto-reselect from dead 7999 to healthy 8005, then force offline 8005 and observe fallback.
tcp.caseReselectTitle: Scenario B: TCP connect failure to a pool member — auto Retry (in-pool Reselect to another member)
tcp.caseReselectDesc: This test simulates a member that appears selectable to F5 but does not actually serve traffic: in pool_deepseek-chat, member 7999 has no listener, causing TCP connection failure. F5 performs in-pool member reselection and switches traffic to a healthy member.
tcp.caseReselectExpected: Expected validation: requests finally return from member 8005 (server_port=8005), proving in-pool reselection instead of cross-pool fallback.
tcp.caseFallbackTitle: Scenario C: Target model pool fully unavailable — auto Fallback to default pool
tcp.caseFallbackDesc: This test forces member 8005 offline so all members in pool_deepseek-chat become unavailable. Once in-pool reselection is exhausted, policy triggers fallback to the default pool (pool_llm_default).
tcp.caseFallbackExpected: Expected validation: final response indicates pool_llm_default (or terminal retry/upstream_error), confirming cross-pool fallback.
tcp.expectedPort: Expected all requests to end on server_port={{port}}
tcp.fallbackToDefault: Fallback to default pool detected (default_model mismatch).
tcp.terminalFallback: Terminal retry response detected (all members unavailable / terminal header).
tcp.stabilityWait: Pool member just recovered — waiting for stability (3s)…

retryFallback.title: Retry & Fallback (logic in this scenario)
retryFallback.subtitle: Router and TBLB work in layers: pick a pool, then a member, then escalate on failure. This describes behavior only—not internal implementation.
retryFallback.step1Body: Based on model (and context / agent rules), traffic is steered to a target pool, e.g. pool_gpt-4o.
retryFallback.step2Title: Pick a member inside the pool
retryFallback.step2Body: TBLB-enabled pools: Scheduler picks the best member from queue/cache metrics. Other pools: standard pool load balancing.
retryFallback.step3Body: If the chosen member is TCP-unreachable (LB_FAILED), F5 tries another member in the same pool before crossing pools.
retryFallback.step4Title: 5xx / 429 or members exhausted → Router retry + cross-pool fallback
retryFallback.step4Body: HTTP status codes trigger limited Router retries; if the primary pool still fails, traffic falls back to the configured default pool (e.g. pool_llm_default).
retryFallback.sameAsRouterTitle: Router-layer Retry / Fallback demo is separate from the TBLB demo above
retryFallback.sameAsRouterBody: Steps 3 (in-pool reselect) and 4 (5xx retry + cross-pool fallback) are demonstrated in Scene 1 · LLM Router → Retry & Fallback—same VS, same pools, same demo buttons. This page only covers TBLB member scheduling (step 2) and does not duplicate those tests.
retryFallback.goToRouterDemo: Go to LLM Router · Retry & Fallback demo →
retryFallback.footnote: TBLB’s difference is metric-driven routing in step 2. Steps 3–4 are provided by Router + LTM regardless of whether TBLB is enabled.
